prompt: Lesson 1 already purged the FTP server. What does a default-deny firewall add on top?

choices.text: Nothing: once the listener is gone a filter is redundant
choices.why: It covers the listener nobody has installed yet.

choices.text: Protection against tomorrow's listener
choices.why: Right. A new service stays unreachable until somebody allows it.

choices.text: A patch for any flaw in the services it allows through
choices.why: Allowed services are reachable by design, flaws included.

choices.text: Encryption for the HTTP traffic the portal serves
choices.why: A filter decides, it does not encrypt.

prompt: What does default deny mean for a rule set?

choices.text: Every rule in it ends with drop
choices.why: The rules above are permissions; only the end drops.

choices.text: It denies the known attacks and accepts the rest
choices.why: That is the opposite, default allow.

choices.text: What no rule allows is dropped
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nobody may change it without a second administrator's approval
choices.why: That is change control, not the rule set's shape.

prompt: Why does the rule set accept `ct state established,related` near the top?

choices.text: So replies to allowed connections need no rule of their own
choices.why: Right. Each permission is written once.

choices.text: To let administrators in even when SSH is not listed
choices.why: A new SSH connection is not established; it still needs its rule.

choices.text: Because nftables refuses a policy drop without it
choices.why: It accepts it; replies would just be dropped.

choices.text: To speed up loopback traffic between nginx and the portal
choices.why: The loopback has its own rule.

prompt: What would break on web if the rule `iif "lo" accept` were missing?

choices.text: Ping from admin
choices.why: Ping has its own rule and comes over eth0.

choices.text: nginx reaching the portal on 127.0.0.1:8080
choices.why: Right. That conversation never leaves the machine.

choices.text: SSH from jump, which arrives through the loopback interface
choices.why: jump's packets arrive on eth0 like any other machine's.

choices.text: Nothing, since loopback traffic never passes the input hook
choices.why: It does pass input, which is why the rule exists.

prompt: What does `nft -c -f nftables.conf` do?

choices.text: Loads the rules and keeps a copy of the old ones
choices.why: -c installs nothing.

choices.text: Checks the file without installing it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Counts the packets each rule would match
choices.why: Counters count after loading.

choices.text: Converts the file to iptables syntax
choices.why: That is iptables-translate's job.

prompt: After the rule set is loaded, `ss` on web still counts six listeners. What does that mean?

choices.text: The rule set did not load, because ss would count two otherwise
choices.why: ss shows sockets, which a firewall does not touch.

choices.text: The firewall only applies after the services restart
choices.why: It applied at once, as desk saw.

choices.text: The services still run, only unreachable
choices.why: Right. Which is why removing them still matters.

choices.text: Six machines are connected to web right now
choices.why: -l lists listening sockets, not connections.

prompt: With `counter reject`, nc reports Connection refused but nmap still says filtered. Why?

choices.text: nmap scanned before the reject rule was loaded
choices.why: It ran after, in the same block.

choices.text: The ICMP unreachable reads to nmap as a firewall's answer
choices.why: Right. A TCP reset is what nmap calls closed.

choices.text: nc and nmap use different ports for the same service
choices.why: Both asked port 21.

choices.text: reject drops packets from nmap but answers nc
choices.why: The rule cannot tell one client program from another.

prompt: With the drop policy, how many seconds did `nc -zv -w3 web 21` take before giving up?
After `systemctl restart nftables`, the reject rule loaded by hand earlier is gone. Why?

choices.text: Restarting the service wipes every firewall rule and loads nothing
choices.why: It loaded the file: the policy drop is there.

choices.text: The service loads the file, which never held it
choices.why: Right. What is in the file is what runs after a reboot.

choices.text: reject rules expire after a few minutes
choices.why: Rules do not expire.

choices.text: ufw removed it when the service restarted
choices.why: ufw is inactive on web.

prompt: A colleague enables ufw on web while nftables.service also loads /etc/nftables.conf. What is the risk?

choices.text: None: ufw only writes rules for IPv6
choices.why: It writes rules for both.

choices.text: The kernel refuses to load two rule sets and keeps the first
choices.why: The kernel accepts both; they interact.

choices.text: Two tools that each believe they own the rule set
choices.why: Right. One undoes the other; nft list ruleset shows what is real.

choices.text: ufw blocks port 80 by default and the portal goes offline
choices.why: The risk is not one port; it is two owners.

prompt: Why does removing the usb-storage driver not stop a device that announces itself as a keyboard?

choices.text: Because keyboards use Bluetooth, not USB
choices.why: Plenty are USB; this one is.

choices.text: Typing goes through the input layer, not storage
choices.why: Right. Only a device allow-list decides on class.

choices.text: Because the driver is reloaded every time a key is pressed
choices.why: Drivers are not reloaded per keystroke.

choices.text: Because the keyboard copies files faster than a stick
choices.why: A keyboard copies no files; it types.

prompt: Read-only removable storage stops which of the three risks?

choices.text: Malware arriving on a stick
choices.why: Reading a file is how it arrives.

choices.text: Data leaving on a stick
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A device posing as a keyboard
choices.why: It needs no storage at all.

choices.text: All three, because nothing can be written to the machine
choices.why: Read-only applies to the stick, and stops one thing.

prompt: Why was the USBGuard policy not built in the lab?

choices.text: USBGuard is not in Ubuntu's archive
choices.why: It is installed on every lab machine.

choices.text: It needs a licence the course does not ask for
choices.why: It is free software.

choices.text: A container has no USB bus to read
choices.why: Right. /sys/bus/usb does not exist inside it.

choices.text: USBGuard only runs on desktop editions of Ubuntu
choices.why: It runs on servers too; the container is the problem.

prompt: What does `install usb-storage /bin/false` add to `blacklist usb-storage`?

choices.text: Even a manual modprobe of the module fails
choices.why: Right. blacklist only stops automatic loading.

choices.text: It unloads the module if it is already loaded
choices.why: A loaded module stays until removed or a reboot.

choices.text: It blocks keyboards as well as storage
choices.why: It touches only usb-storage.

choices.text: It logs every stick that is plugged in
choices.why: Nothing in it logs.

prompt: A device with an allowed stick's vendor and product id also presents an interface of class 03. Against a rule with `with-interface 08:06:50`, what happens?

choices.text: It is allowed, because the ids match
choices.why: The interfaces must match too.

choices.text: It does not match, and falls to block
choices.why: Right. The extra keyboard interface is the giveaway.

choices.text: Only its storage interface is allowed, and the keyboard part works anyway
choices.why: A rule matches a device, not half of one.

choices.text: USBGuard asks the user whether to allow it
choices.why: The rule list decides; nobody is asked.

How many `accept` rules does the portal's rule set contain?
A chain whose last word is `policy ___` discards every packet no rule accepted.
Which statements are true of this lesson's firewall? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Only .30 and .40 may connect.

choices.text: It filters what web sends to other machines
choices.why: Only input; output is lesson 10.

choices.text: It removed the FTP server from web
